CARES Security Architecture

Status: proposed target controls only. This document describes NOT IMPLEMENTED and NOT TESTED security architecture and controls unless actual repository evidence proves otherwise. The current repository has no web/API boundary, identity provider, database, network listener, agent, secret store, logging system, verified-context implementation, RLS policies, forensic evidence implementation, or production deployment. No security control described here is implemented, verified, or certified.

Security objectives and trust boundaries

  • Authenticate users, agents, and integrations independently.
  • Derive tenant authority from trusted identity/membership records and verified transaction context, never from an untrusted request body, client-supplied tenant identifier, user-settable custom GUC, or model response.
  • Enforce tenant scope in service logic and PostgreSQL RLS using protected, verified transaction context.
  • Protect secrets, event data, telemetry, backups, evidence, and AI prompts according to classification and retention policy.
  • Make privileged access, configuration changes, controlled evidence transitions, and support actions attributable and auditable.
  • Make MELIRA optional and prevent it from becoming an authorization or autonomous action authority.

Verified transaction context and tenant isolation

Tenant isolation must not rely on a tenant identifier supplied directly by an untrusted API request, client payload, or user-settable custom PostgreSQL GUC. SET app.tenant_id or any other custom GUC is not an authorization boundary and must never be read by RLS policies, authorization helpers, or controlled-transition logic for allow/deny decisions. Custom GUCs may be used only for non-authoritative diagnostics if explicitly approved.

Signed tenant assertion verification (proposed)

Before tenant-scoped database access, a trusted verifier must validate a signed tenant assertion and establish protected transaction-bound verified context:

  • Signature and key state: verify signature, algorithm, and signing key status; reject unknown, inactive, or revoked keys.
  • Issuer and audience: validate trusted issuer and expected audience/service binding.
  • Principal and service identity: validate authenticated principal/service identity and actor type; context must not be derived from client-claimed identity alone.
  • Tenant and scopes: validate target tenant and allowed scopes/actions required for the operation; requested scope must be within the verified assertion scope.
  • Nonce and replay protection: validate nonce/token identifier and enforce atomic single-use/replay-prevention semantics per approved protocol.
  • Expiry and time bounds: validate issuance/validity/expiry and approved clock-skew handling; reject expired, not-yet-valid, or ambiguous assertions.
  • Request/job binding: bind context to the specific request or job context where required by the approved design.

Protected transaction-bound verified context and RLS (proposed)

  • The verifier writes verified claims only to a protected, security-internal, transaction-bound context (not to an authorization GUC). Ordinary runtime, worker, ingest, reader, and administrative application roles must not be able to insert, update, delete, or forge that context.
  • RLS and authorization helpers must obtain tenant/scope decisions only from trusted verified context through narrowly scoped, hardened SECURITY DEFINER helpers that return only required decisions/values (for example validity, verified tenant, and scope allowance), not full sensitive context records to ordinary roles.
  • RLS design must follow the latest architecture decision package: restrictive tenant boundary policies, permissive gate/action policies as required, command-specific enforcement for SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, fail-closed behavior on missing/invalid context, and no reliance on BYPASSRLS for ordinary runtime paths.
  • Service-layer authorization checks remain required; RLS is defense in depth, not a substitute for authentication, application authorization, or safe SQL design.

Connection-pool isolation and cleanup (proposed)

  • Each tenant-scoped transaction must establish its own verified context and must not inherit context from a pooled session or previous transaction.
  • Context must be bound to the current transaction/backend/binding epoch (or approved equivalent) so stale rows cannot authorize later transactions, including after backend PID or transaction-identifier reuse.
  • Explicit cleanup and/or transaction-end teardown must remove current-transaction authorization state as designed; maintenance cleanup may remove only provably stale/inactive records per approved rules. Missing reset/cleanup certainty requires connection discard and fail-closed behavior.
  • Pool/session abandonment, rollback, commit, and unknown-commit outcomes must not leave reusable authorization.

Fail-closed behavior (proposed)

Missing, invalid, expired, revoked, replayed, malformed, wrong-audience, wrong-issuer, wrong-tenant, wrong-scope, wrong-transaction, wrong-binding, or unverifiable assertions/contexts must deny access. Failures must be audited with sanitized details (no secrets, full tokens, or sensitive claim leakage).

Relationship to JIT support authorization (proposed)

JIT support access is not blanket tenant membership and not BYPASSRLS. A support action requires an explicit, time-bound, scoped, reasoned, and audited authorization/grant approved through the trusted authorization path. The resulting database context, if any, must still be represented as verified transaction-bound context with the specific tenant and permitted support scope for that transaction/request; RLS and audit controls remain enforced.

PostgreSQL privilege separation and RLS posture (proposed)

Logical PostgreSQL role separation (privilege boundaries, not necessarily separate applications):

Logical role Primary responsibility Least-privilege intent
cares_api_runtime Tenant-scoped API/application request execution after verified context establishment Only required DML/SELECT on approved application objects for API paths; no schema ownership, no security-function ownership, no direct access to security-internal context/authorization tables except through approved narrow helpers/call paths
cares_ingest_runtime Tenant-scoped ingestion/enrollment/event processing after verified context establishment Only required ingest-path privileges; no broad administrative, migration, or security-definition rights
cares_worker_runtime Background job/outbox/processing execution with its own verified context per transaction/job Only required worker-path privileges; no direct evidence/security bypass, no schema/security ownership; outbox claim/replay semantics must follow approved scope-specific design (event-processing vs controlled/external-side-effect delivery)
cares_migration Controlled schema migration and deployment-time DDL changes Migration-time privileges only; not used for ordinary runtime traffic; access controlled, reviewed, and audited
cares_maintenance Controlled maintenance tasks (for example approved cleanup/vacuum/index/reconciliation operations) under explicit procedures Narrow maintenance privileges only; cannot bypass tenant authorization controls except where explicitly approved, separately controlled, and audited

Explicit prohibitions for ordinary runtime roles (cares_api_runtime, cares_ingest_runtime, cares_worker_runtime):

  • Must not be SUPERUSER.
  • Must not have BYPASSRLS.
  • Must not own protected application tables, security-internal tables, RLS policies, or security-critical functions/procedures/triggers.
  • Must not create/alter/own/grant roles, policies, extensions, or security-definer objects.
  • Must not have direct ad hoc access to protected transaction-context, nonce, or evidence-transition authorization tables except through approved, hardened, narrowly scoped interfaces where required.

Additional restrictions (proposed):

  • Direct access to partitioned child tables must be restricted and reviewed; ordinary runtime access should use approved parent-table/query paths and RLS-safe interfaces to prevent bypass or inconsistent enforcement.
  • Maintenance operations (partition management, cleanup, reindexing, vacuum/analyze where elevated behavior is involved, reconciliation, retention/purge execution) must run under controlled cares_maintenance or separately approved procedures with least privilege, change control, and auditability; no silent data deletion or bypass of legal holds/evidence controls.
  • Consistency with latest RLS design: restrictive tenant boundary policies enforce tenant isolation; permissive gate policies and action/scope policies (as approved) must not weaken tenant boundaries. SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE are independently controlled as required. Apply ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and, where applicable and ownership/role design permits, FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on tenant/protected tables; exact applicability requires formal PostgreSQL schema/security review. BYPASSRLS is restricted to explicitly approved, separately controlled non-runtime roles/processes only. UPDATE/SELECT/RETURNING interactions and required read visibility for row-addressed workflows must be designed explicitly (see DATA_ARCHITECTURE.md and ARCHITECTURE_DECISION_PACKAGE_FINAL_CORRECTIONS.md).

Device identity, agent identity, and licensing integrity

Identity distinctions (proposed)

  • Agent identity: the authenticated runtime identity of a CARES agent instance/process as recognized by the platform (separate from the device it reports and from user identity).
  • Enrollment credential: the credential/material used during enrollment or re-enrollment to establish or prove agent trust; short-lived/single-use where applicable and rotatable/revocable.
  • Connector/source identity (data_source/connector instance): the tenant-scoped integration or collection channel/instance that submits data; it is not a billable asset and may report one or many devices.
  • Source-device identity / source-device binding: the source-local device identity as known to a specific connector/source, represented by tenant-scoped bindings (including asset_data_source and versioned fingerprint aliases as designed) and provenance/confidence.
  • Canonical CARES asset identity: the tenant-scoped canonical monitored-asset identity representing one unique monitored device (physical or logical). It is the licensing/billing identity, not a connector and not a raw source identifier.

Binding, lifecycle, and licensing effects (proposed)

  • Multiple connectors/sources reporting the same device must bind to one canonical CARES asset and must not create duplicate licensed assets.
  • Agent reinstall, replacement, or re-enrollment affects agent identity/enrollment credentials and may require new or updated source-device bindings/claims; it does not automatically create a duplicate licensed asset. Identity resolution must follow approved authoritative/strong/weak evidence rules, with conflict/pending review where required.
  • Credential rotation and revocation invalidate or replace affected credentials/agent trust material without automatically deleting canonical asset history or creating duplicate assets; re-enrollment must be authorized and auditable.
  • Source identifiers remain untrusted claims until bound to an authenticated tenant and source. Namespace, provenance, and confidence must be preserved. IP addresses and hostnames are observations only; weak matches never merge automatically.
  • Manual merge/split must be tenant-scoped, permission-checked, reasoned, auditable, and transactional. Preserve canonical IDs, source/event lineage, before/after claims, and evidence history. Split/merge quota and licensing effects must be handled atomically per approved rules; compensating actions must preserve history.
  • Use tenant-inclusive constraints/relationships (including stable asset_data_source bindings, source_device_key_id, and versioned source_device_fingerprint_alias records as designed), scope-appropriate idempotency (ingestion event_receipt, licensing/identity operation ledger, and outbox attempt/replay records), per-tenant serialized quota operations, and reconciliation to limit spoofing, duplicate billing, and race abuse. See DATA_ARCHITECTURE.md, docs/adr/0006-atomic-per-tenant-asset-licensing.md, and POSTGRESQL_TECHNICAL_DECISIONS.md.

Agent and integration security (proposed)

Use short-lived, single-use enrollment where applicable, tenant-bound unique credentials, mutual TLS or equivalent strong client authentication, rotation/revocation, replay-resistant idempotency, and per-source rate/payload limits. Agent offline queues must be bounded and encrypted where feasible. Commands and updates require signatures, expiry, target binding, and anti-replay protections. Do not accept arbitrary shell commands as a generic integration mechanism.

For integrations, store credentials as secret references, restrict egress, validate webhooks and signatures, and isolate adapter parsing from trusted control messages. Treat all third-party event content as attacker-controlled data.

Data protection, audit, and forensic evidence (proposed)

Use TLS in transit, encryption at rest for database and backups (where implemented), least-privilege service identities, controlled key rotation, and documented retention/deletion. Minimize PII in metrics and logs.

Distinction of record types

Record type Purpose Integrity/protection expectations Access/authorization Retention/lifecycle
Operational/security audit records Accountability for administrative, customer-sensitive, security, AI, configuration, access, and response actions Protected from ordinary application modification/tampering; attributable actor/tenant/action/target/reason/outcome/correlation; append-oriented or otherwise integrity-protected logging as approved Least-privilege read/access for authorized roles; alerting/review as required Retention per approved security/compliance policy; not silently deleted
Forensic evidence metadata and objects Preserved evidence artifacts and their authoritative metadata for investigation/forensics/legal support Immutable evidence metadata and original evidence objects/hashes/provenance as designed; controlled transitions only; hash verification; tenant-scoped evidence references; original evidence never silently rewritten or deleted Strict tenant-scoped, purpose-limited authorization; controlled procedures only for allowed state transitions Retention/legal hold/deletion/purge governed by approved policy; legal hold prevents unauthorized disposal
Evidence custody events Chain-of-custody and controlled-transition history for evidence Append-only custody events with required sequencing/linkage as designed; transaction-bound authorized transitions; no ad hoc update/delete by ordinary runtime/worker/admin application roles Restricted to authorized ingestion/controlled procedures and approved readers/auditors Retained per approved evidence/audit policy; integrity verification required before trusted use where applicable

Evidence controls (proposed, aligned with latest architecture decisions)

  • Immutable evidence metadata: immutable identity/object/hash/provenance/source/ingest fields must not be directly modified or deleted.
  • Controlled evidence transitions: only approved, hardened SECURITY DEFINER procedures may perform allowed transitions (for example legal hold, retention metadata, and availability-state changes) with precondition checks and required custody events.
  • Transaction-bound authorization: controlled transitions require protected, security-internal, transaction-bound authorization records bound to current transaction/binding, tenant, evidence record, and permitted operation/transition; custom GUC values are not proof of authorization. Authorization creation, controlled update, custody-event append, and single-use authorization consumption must be atomic in the same transaction; rollback leaves no reusable authorization.
  • Append-only custody events: custody events are append-only with required per-evidence sequencing/hash linkage as designed; direct update/delete prohibited for ordinary roles.
  • Evidence hash verification: verify object/content hashes and custody linkage before trusted use/delivery where required; integrity failures must be handled through controlled procedures and audited.
  • Legal hold: legal hold and retention controls prevent unauthorized purge/deletion and require approved handling.
  • Tenant-scoped evidence references: evidence metadata, objects, custody events, and references must be tenant-scoped and access-controlled.

Integrity limitation and additional controls (proposed)

A database hash chain alone is not independently tamper-proof against privileged database administrators or other actors with sufficient database/platform control; it provides tamper-evidence within the database trust boundary, not independent assurance. External immutable storage/WORM/object-lock or equivalent independent integrity controls are potential additional controls requiring owner/security approval, implementation design, and verification.

MELIRA external provider security and privacy boundary (proposed)

Before any network request to an AI SaaS provider:

  1. Re-authenticate/authorize the user, tenant, operation, and each requested tool.
  2. Fetch only evidence authorized for that tenant and purpose.
  3. Require an administrator-configured provider/model/approved region and explicit customer agreement to provider terms. Proposed default is no provider and no transmission until configured; AI requests are user-initiated with an external-processing notice, not background export. No selection, disabled configuration, absent consent, or denied policy means no provider call.
  4. Classify data and apply per-tenant classification, transmission, file-content, minimization, retention, and usage policies. Proposed defaults deny restricted data, secrets, credentials, and file content; confidential data is denied unless separately authorized; public/internal data still requires tenant opt-in and minimization. The exact matrix and consent granularity require owner/privacy/legal approval. Treat free-form logs as untrusted data, not instructions.
  5. Check the provider's documented residency, retention/deletion, and training/data-use terms against the tenant's policy. If requirements cannot be verified or are incompatible, block transmission. No local inference and no silent provider/region failover.
  6. Call only an explicitly selected, approved endpoint over validated HTTPS with the following controls (a one-time DNS lookup is not sufficient protection):
    • TLS hostname verification: enforce certificate validation and hostname verification for the approved destination.
    • DNS and connection-time destination IP validation: resolve and validate destination addresses and revalidate as required; reject loopback, private, link-local, multicast, unspecified, and cloud metadata addresses and other disallowed targets.
    • DNS rebinding resistance: do not trust earlier resolution results across validation/use boundaries without approved revalidation; prevent rebinding to disallowed internal/metadata targets.
    • Redirect handling and revalidation: do not follow redirects to unapproved destinations; if redirects are handled at all under approved policy, revalidate scheme, host, TLS hostname, resolved IPs, and allow-list/egress policy on every hop and prefer disabling redirects.
    • Egress firewall enforcement: enforce network egress allow-lists/deny-lists and controls so only approved provider destinations/ports are reachable.
    • Custom provider endpoint approval: custom endpoints require a separately approved allow-list/security review path and must satisfy the same validation controls.
    • No automatic provider or region failover: never automatically switch provider, endpoint, or region on error/policy failure.
  7. Fetch the credential through a tenant-scoped secret reference from the secret manager. Never return credentials to the UI or put them in prompts/logs. Audit secret reads and rotation/revocation.
  8. Enforce hard per-tenant request/token/spend/concurrency budgets using a preflight estimate and actual usage reconciliation. Fail closed if budget status is unavailable or exhausted. Report provider errors explicitly; never switch providers automatically.
  9. Treat model output as untrusted. Validate each tool, tenant, target, and argument against CARES authorization independently of the model. Default to read-only; require human approval for high-impact changes.
  10. Record tenant, actor, purpose, provider/model/region, policy/catalog version, data classifications/categories, evidence IDs, estimated/actual usage and cost, outcome, and correlation ID. Do not retain full prompts/responses by default.

Protect against prompt injection by separating instructions from quoted evidence and by denying event/file content authority to issue instructions. This mitigates but cannot eliminate model behavior risk. Maintain core detection and response functions without the AI service.

The supported provider list, allowed data classification per provider, consent roles, customer BYOK versus CARES-managed key custody, residency regions, acceptable retention/training terms, and budget ceilings require owner/privacy/legal approval. The control sequence is proposed only; no provider integration exists and local inference is not permitted.

Security control status

Proposed controls must be implemented and verified through API, DB/RLS, integration, and adversarial tests before any production security claim. The current AccessController is a comparison helper; the current AI classes only calculate a local status and string transform. Neither is an actual security boundary.

All controls in this document remain proposed and unimplemented unless actual repository evidence proves otherwise. No source code, schema, migration, or test files were modified by this documentation update.
